A throttle (default 1024 rows) keeps small tasks on one thread, and data.table switches to a single thread inside a forked process (the mechanism of parallel::mclapply()), so it does not oversubscribe the CPUs of code that is already parallel. CRAN’s own checks set OMP_THREAD_LIMIT to 2, and a package must not raise it above 2. See Parallel and Asynchronous Computing for the other parallel tools.

suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(data.table))
source("scenario.R")
setDT(loans)

# The defaults of the printing options in this version.
str(options("datatable.print.nrows", "datatable.print.topn",
            "datatable.print.class", "datatable.print.keys"))
#> List of 4
#>  $ datatable.print.nrows: int 100
#>  $ datatable.print.topn : int 5
#>  $ datatable.print.class: logi TRUE
#>  $ datatable.print.keys : logi TRUE

# A table longer than nrows (100) prints its first and last topn (5) rows.
data.table(n = 1:150, square = (1:150)^2)
#>          n square
#>      <int>  <num>
#>   1:     1      1
#>   2:     2      4
#>   3:     3      9
#>   4:     4     16
#>   5:     5     25
#>  ---
#> 146:   146  21316
#> 147:   147  21609
#> 148:   148  21904
#> 149:   149  22201
#> 150:   150  22500

# nrows and topn can be given to print() for a single call.
print(loans[, .(loan_id, member)], nrows = 8, topn = 2)
#>     loan_id     member
#>      <char>     <char>
#>  1:    L001 Hugo Silva
#>  2:    L002 Ben Okafor
#> ---
#> 59:    L059   Ana Ruiz
#> 60:    L060 Hugo Silva

# Other arguments: no row numbers, no class line, no column names.
print(loans[1:3, .(loan_id, member)], row.names = FALSE)
#>  loan_id     member
#>   <char>     <char>
#>     L001 Hugo Silva
#>     L002 Ben Okafor
#>     L003  Dev Patel
print(loans[1:3, .(loan_id, member)], class = FALSE)
#>    loan_id     member
#> 1:    L001 Hugo Silva
#> 2:    L002 Ben Okafor
#> 3:    L003  Dev Patel
print(loans[1:3, .(loan_id, member)], class = FALSE, col.names = "none")
#> 1: L001 Hugo Silva
#> 2: L002 Ben Okafor
#> 3: L003  Dev Patel

# The same settings as options apply to every table of the session.
options(datatable.print.nrows = 5, datatable.print.topn = 1,
        datatable.print.class = FALSE)
loans[, .(loan_id, member)]
#>     loan_id     member
#>  1:    L001 Hugo Silva
#> ---
#> 60:    L060 Hugo Silva
options(datatable.print.nrows = 100, datatable.print.topn = 5,
        datatable.print.class = TRUE)

# Threads: data.table uses OpenMP threads for fread(), fwrite(), sorting and
# grouping. The number depends on the machine, so only a check is shown.
getDTthreads() >= 1L
#> [1] TRUE
old <- setDTthreads(1L)
getDTthreads()
#> [1] 1
invisible(setDTthreads(old))
getDTthreads() == old
#> [1] TRUE

Source: data.table package documentation: print.data.table

Source: data.table package documentation: setDTthreads and getDTthreads

The shelf analyses with data.table

The analyses of Data Frames are rewritten here, and the numbers are the same: nine spellings of six genres, 32 overdue loans, 27 that are not and one that cannot be told, and an overdue rate by genre that runs from 0.67 for poetry to 0.47 for science fiction. Each script repeats its own setup and can be run alone.

Cleaning the books and the loans

One := call cleans four columns of books: it trims the blanks of title, author and genre, collapses the repeated blanks of the author (gsub("\\s+", " ", ...)), lower-cases the genre, and keeps only the digits and X of the ISBN. The two spellings of Ursula K. Le Guin remain, as in the base-R page: no rule fixes them. For the loans, tools::toTitleCase() repairs the member names and the empty name becomes NA; the dates are converted from the character columns of the scenario, and the rows that need a decision are listed.

suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(data.table))
source("scenario.R")
setDT(books)
setDT(loans)

# books: nine spellings of six genres, padded titles, two spellings of Le Guin.
books[, .N, by = genre][order(genre)]
#>              genre     N
#>             <char> <int>
#> 1:         Classic     2
#> 2:         Fiction     2
#> 3:        Fiction      1
#> 4:         Mystery     2
#> 5:     Non-fiction     3
#> 6:          Poetry     2
#> 7: Science fiction     2
#> 8:         fiction     1
#> 9: science fiction     1

# Clean in place with one := call; the isbn keeps only digits and X.
books[, `:=`(
  title = trimws(title),
  author = gsub("\\s+", " ", trimws(author)),
  genre = tolower(trimws(genre)),
  isbn = gsub("[^0-9X]", "", toupper(isbn))
)]
books[, .N, by = genre][order(genre)]
#>              genre     N
#>             <char> <int>
#> 1:         classic     2
#> 2:         fiction     4
#> 3:         mystery     2
#> 4:     non-fiction     3
#> 5:          poetry     2
#> 6: science fiction     3
books[c(3, 10), .(title, author)]
#>                title       author
#>               <char>       <char>
#> 1: the quiet streets   Mara Quill
#> 2:    THE LONG TABLE Iris Fenwick

# loans: member names differ in case and padding, and one is empty.
loans[, member := tools::toTitleCase(trimws(member))]
loans[!nzchar(member), member := NA]
sort(unique(loans$member))
#> [1] "Ana Ruiz"      "Ben Okafor"    "Chloe Martin"  "Dev Patel"
#> [5] "Eva Lindqvist" "Farid Karimi"  "Grace Liu"     "Hugo Silva"

# Rows that need a look: a loan returned before it was made, an impossible
# date (2025-02-30 is NA after the conversion).
loans[, `:=`(
  loan_date = as.Date(loan_date),
  return_date = as.Date(return_date)
)]
loans[return_date < loan_date | is.na(loan_date),
      .(loan_id, loan_date, return_date)]
#>    loan_id  loan_date return_date
#>     <char>     <Date>      <Date>
#> 1:    L012 2025-04-23  2025-04-20
#> 2:    L020       <NA>  2025-07-15

Source: data.table package documentation: := (assign)

Overdue loans

A loan is overdue when it was held for more than loan_days (21) days: until the return date when there is one, and until shelf_today (2026-06-30) when the book is still out. fifelse() picks the end date and keeps its class, so the subtraction is between dates. The counts agree with the base-R page (27, 32 and 1), and the remaining overdue loans are the books to chase.

suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(data.table))
source("scenario.R")
setDT(loans)
loans[, `:=`(
  loan_date = as.Date(loan_date),
  return_date = as.Date(return_date)
)]

# Days held: until the return date, or until shelf_today when still out.
loans[, held := as.integer(fifelse(is.na(return_date), shelf_today,
                                   return_date) - loan_date)]
loans[, overdue := held > loan_days]
loans[1:4, .(loan_id, held, overdue)]
#>    loan_id  held overdue
#>     <char> <int>  <lgcl>
#> 1:    L001    21   FALSE
#> 2:    L002    10   FALSE
#> 3:    L003     1   FALSE
#> 4:    L004    26    TRUE
loans[, .N, by = overdue][order(overdue)]
#>    overdue     N
#>     <lgcl> <int>
#> 1:   FALSE    27
#> 2:    TRUE    32
#> 3:      NA     1

# Overdue loans that are still out: the books to chase.
still_out <- loans[is.na(return_date) & overdue,
                   .(loan_id, member, loan_date, held)]
still_out[order(-held)][1:4]
#>    loan_id        member  loan_date  held
#>     <char>        <char>     <Date> <int>
#> 1:    L054  Chloe Martin 2026-04-07    84
#> 2:    L055 Eva Lindqvist 2026-04-10    81
#> 3:    L056     Dev Patel 2026-04-20    71
#> 4:    L057     Dev Patel 2026-04-26    65

# Overdue returned loans per member, most first (the loan without a member
# is left out).
per_member <- loans[!is.na(member) & overdue, .(overdue = .N), by = member]
per_member[order(-overdue, member)][1:3]
#>          member overdue
#>          <char>   <int>
#> 1: Chloe Martin       6
#> 2:     Ana Ruiz       5
#> 3:   Hugo Silva       5

Source: data.table package documentation: fifelse

Loans per month and the overdue rate by genre

keyby sorts the months and sets the key; the busiest months are July and October 2025 with seven loans each, as in the chart of Base Graphics and Devices. The overdue rate joins the loans to the books with books[loans, on = "isbn", nomatch = NULL], which keeps the 59 loans that match a book; dropping the one whose overdue flag is NA leaves the 58 loans of the base-R page, and the table is the same as its merge() and aggregate() result, from poetry (4 of 6) to science fiction (7 of 15).

suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(data.table))
source("scenario.R")
setDT(books)
setDT(loans)
books[, `:=`(
  title = trimws(title),
  genre = tolower(trimws(genre)),
  isbn = gsub("[^0-9X]", "", toupper(isbn))
)]
loans[, `:=`(
  loan_date = as.Date(loan_date),
  return_date = as.Date(return_date)
)]
loans[, held := as.integer(fifelse(is.na(return_date), shelf_today,
                                   return_date) - loan_date)]
loans[, overdue := held > loan_days]

# Loans per month; keyby sorts the months and the NA date is left out.
per_month <- loans[!is.na(loan_date), .N,
                   keyby = .(month = format(loan_date, "%Y-%m"))]
per_month[N == max(N)]
#> Key: <month>
#>      month     N
#>     <char> <int>
#> 1: 2025-07     7
#> 2: 2025-10     7
per_month[1:3]
#> Key: <month>
#>      month     N
#>     <char> <int>
#> 1: 2025-01     4
#> 2: 2025-02     2
#> 3: 2025-03     3

# Join the loans to the books, then the overdue rate by genre.
joined <- books[loans, on = "isbn", nomatch = NULL]
by_genre <- joined[!is.na(overdue), .(loans = .N, overdue = sum(overdue)),
                   by = genre]
by_genre[, share := round(overdue / loans, 2)]
by_genre[order(-share, genre)]
#>              genre loans overdue share
#>             <char> <int>   <int> <num>
#> 1:          poetry     6       4  0.67
#> 2:         classic     5       3  0.60
#> 3:     non-fiction     5       3  0.60
#> 4:         fiction    23      12  0.52
#> 5:         mystery     4       2  0.50
#> 6: science fiction    15       7  0.47

# The three titles loaned most often.
joined[, .N, by = title][order(-N, title)][1:3]
#>                title     N
#>               <char> <int>
#> 1: the quiet streets     8
#> 2:       Ten Winters     7
#> 3:  The Dispossessed     7

Source: data.table package documentation: Introduction to data.table

data.table or dplyr?

The two packages answer the same question, how to write a table transformation as a short, readable pipeline, and both are valid choices. They differ in the vocabulary, in the treatment of the table, and in the cost of a wrong guess. The table lines up the same operations in base R (the functions of Data Frames), dplyr (the verbs of The tidyverse and dplyr, following the official dplyr vignette on base R equivalents) and data.table.

Task base R dplyr data.table

read a CSV

read.csv("books.csv")

readr::read_csv("books.csv")

fread("books.csv")

filter(books, year > 2020)

books[year > 2020]

books[, .(title, year)]

books$age <- 2026L - books$year

mutate(books, age = 2026L - year)

books[, age := 2026L - year] (in place)

change some rows

books$pages[books$pages > 400] <- 400L

mutate(books, pages = if_else(pages > 400, 400L, pages))

books[pages > 400, pages := 400L] (in place)

summarise

mean(books$pages, na.rm = TRUE)

summarise(books, avg = mean(pages, na.rm = TRUE))

books[loans, on = "isbn"]

Source: dplyr package documentation: dplyr and base R

The script below does not rest on the table: it runs the base-R, dplyr and data.table versions of five of its rows (filter, choose and sort, summarise by group, count by group, inner join) and compares the results by value. dplyr is always called as dplyr::, because attaching it after data.table prints a conflict message for between(), first() and last() (and one for filter() and lag() of the stats package), and the later package hides the earlier one’s functions.

suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(data.table))
source("scenario.R")

# books_df stays a data frame; books_dt is a data.table copy of it.
books$genre <- tolower(trimws(books$genre))
books$isbn <- normalise_isbn(books$isbn)
loans$loan_date <- as.Date(loans$loan_date)
books_df <- books
books_dt <- as.data.table(books)
loans_dt <- as.data.table(loans)

# same() compares two results by value, whatever their class.
same <- \(a, b) {
  isTRUE(all.equal(as.data.frame(a), as.data.frame(b),
                   check.attributes = FALSE))
}

# Filter rows.
r_base <- subset(books_df, year > 2020)
r_dplyr <- dplyr::filter(books_df, year > 2020)
r_dt <- books_dt[year > 2020]
c(same(r_base, r_dplyr), same(r_base, r_dt))
#> [1] TRUE TRUE

# Select columns, then sort (NA last in all three).
r_base <- books_df[order(-books_df$pages), c("title", "pages")]
r_dplyr <- dplyr::arrange(dplyr::select(books_df, title, pages),
                          dplyr::desc(pages))
r_dt <- books_dt[order(-pages), .(title, pages)]
c(same(r_base, r_dplyr), same(r_base, r_dt))
#> [1] TRUE TRUE

# Count and summarise by group.
r_base <- aggregate(pages ~ genre, books_df, \(x) round(mean(x), 1))
r_dplyr <- books_df |>
  dplyr::summarise(pages = round(mean(pages, na.rm = TRUE), 1), .by = genre) |>
  dplyr::arrange(genre)
r_dt <- books_dt[, .(pages = round(mean(pages, na.rm = TRUE), 1)),
                 keyby = genre]
c(same(r_base, r_dplyr), same(r_base, r_dt))
#> [1] TRUE TRUE

n_base <- as.data.frame(table(genre = books_df$genre),
                        responseName = "n", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
n_dplyr <- dplyr::count(books_df, genre)
n_dt <- books_dt[, .(n = .N), keyby = genre]
c(same(n_base, n_dplyr), same(n_base, n_dt))
#> [1] TRUE TRUE

# Join: the loans that match a book, with the title.
j_base <- merge(loans, books_df[c("isbn", "title")], by = "isbn")
j_dplyr <- dplyr::inner_join(loans, books_df[c("isbn", "title")], by = "isbn")
j_dt <- books_dt[, .(isbn, title)][loans_dt, on = "isbn", nomatch = NULL]
sort_ids <- \(d) as.data.frame(d)[order(d$loan_id), c("loan_id", "title")]
c(same(sort_ids(j_base), sort_ids(j_dplyr)),
  same(sort_ids(j_base), sort_ids(j_dt)))
#> [1] TRUE TRUE
nrow(j_base)
#> [1] 59

Source: dplyr package documentation: dplyr and base R

Speed depends on the operation, the size of the data and the machine, so this page prints no timings. The data.table website links to the db-benchmark project (db-benchmark, whose page lists the timings with the syntax timed and the machine type, from 16 cores and 32 GB to 128 cores and 256 GB), and Performance, Profiling and Benchmarking shows how to measure a real case with bench. The differences that do not depend on timings are these:

  • Syntax. dplyr is a set of verbs, each doing one thing, joined with the pipe; data.table is one query form with three slots, in which the work of several verbs fits into one call. The SQL reading of DT[i, j, by] is a way to learn it.

  • Copying. dplyr verbs return a new table and leave the input alone, so a pipeline can be reasoned about step by step; := and the set* functions change the table in place, which saves a copy of a large table and makes it easy to change something the caller did not expect (see Pitfalls).

  • Joins. dplyr has join_by() for equality, inequality, rolling and overlap joins since version 1.1.0 (dplyr package documentation: join_by), so the two cover the same ground; data.table’s on = is terser, and by = .EACHI evaluates j for each row of i, which the error message for an accidental many-to-many join suggests as a way "to avoid the large allocation".

  • Files. fread(data.table = FALSE) returns a plain data frame and fwrite() writes data frames, so the two functions can be used with either package.

  • Dependencies. data.table depends on R 3.4.0 and imports only methods, which ships with R (packageDescription("data.table") in the image used here). dplyr 1.2.1 depends on R 4.1.0 and imports thirteen packages (cli, generics, glue, lifecycle, magrittr, methods, pillar, R6, rlang, tibble, tidyselect, utils and vctrs).

  • Mixing. A data.table is a data frame, so the dplyr verbs accept it, but code that mixes the two vocabularies is read by people who must know both, and a := among pipes can surprise a reader who expects a copy. Teams usually choose one for the main pipeline.

  • dtplyr. The package dtplyr (dtplyr package documentation) is a data.table back end for dplyr: its README states the goal as translating dplyr code into the equivalent data.table code. It is installed in the image used for the examples and is not run on this page.

Common errors and warnings

The messages below are what data.table 1.18.6.1 printed. A helper function runs an expression and prints its first condition as conditionMessage() with error: or warning: in front, wrapped to 76 columns. Many of the messages say what to do next.

suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(data.table))

# what() runs an expression and prints the first condition it signals,
# wrapped to 76 columns (the text is otherwise exactly conditionMessage()).
what <- function(expr) {
  msg <- "no condition"
  withCallingHandlers(
    tryCatch(expr, error = \(e) msg <<- paste("error:", conditionMessage(e))),
    warning = \(w) {
      if (msg == "no condition") {
        msg <<- paste("warning:", conditionMessage(w))
      }
      invokeRestart("muffleWarning")
    }
  )
  cat(strwrap(msg, width = 76, exdent = 2), sep = "\n")
}
new_dt <- \() data.table(a = 1:3, b = c("x", "y", "z"))

# A column that does not exist, in j, in i, and as a selection.
what(new_dt()[, zzz])
#> error: j (the 2nd argument inside [...]) is a single symbol but column name
#>   'zzz' is not found. If you intended to select columns using a variable in
#>   calling scope, please try DT[, ..zzz]. The .. prefix conveys one-level-up
#>   similar to a file system path.
what(new_dt()[, sum(zzz)])
#> error: object 'zzz' not found
what(new_dt()[zzz > 1])
#> error: Object 'zzz' not found amongst [a, b]
what(new_dt()[, c("a", "zzz")])
#> error: column not found: [zzz]
what(new_dt()[, ..zzz])
#> error: Variable 'zzz' is not found in calling scope. Looking in calling
#>   scope because you used the .. prefix.

# Assigning the wrong number of values, or a value of the wrong type.
what(new_dt()[, a := c(1, 2)])
#> error: Supplied 2 items to be assigned to 3 items of column 'a'. If you
#>   wish to 'recycle' the RHS please use rep() to make this intent clear to
#>   readers of your code.
what(new_dt()[1:2, a := "x"])
#> warning: Coercing 'character' RHS to 'integer' to match the type of column
#>   1 named 'a'.
what(new_dt()[, `:=`(p = 1, 2)])
#> error: In `:=`(col1=val1, col2=val2, ...) form, all arguments must be
#>   named, but the last argument has no name. Did you forget a trailing
#>   comma?
what(new_dt()[, zzz := NULL])
#> warning: Tried to assign NULL to column 'zzz', but this column does not
#>   exist to remove

# j that returns different types in different groups.
what(new_dt()[, if (.GRP == 1L) 1 else "a", by = b])
#> error: Column 1 of result for group 2 is type 'character' but expecting
#>   type 'double'. Column types must be consistent for each group.

# A logical i of the wrong length (no recycling).
what(new_dt()[c(TRUE, FALSE)])
#> error: i evaluates to a logical vector length 2 but there are 3 rows.
#>   Recycling of logical i is no longer allowed as it hides more bugs than is
#>   worth the rare convenience. Explicitly use rep(...,length=.N) if you
#>   really need to recycle.

# Names and positions.
what(setnames(new_dt(), "zzz", "q"))
#> error: Items of 'old' not found in column names: [zzz]. Consider
#>   skip_absent=TRUE.
what(setnames(new_dt(), c("p", "q", "r")))
#> error: Can't assign 3 names to a 2-column data.table
what(new_dt()[, 5])
#> error: Item 1 of j is 5 which is outside the column number range [1,ncol=2]
what(setkey(new_dt(), zzz))
#> error: some columns are not in the data.table: [zzz]

Source: data.table package documentation: Frequently asked questions

suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(data.table))
what <- function(expr) {
  msg <- "no condition"
  withCallingHandlers(
    tryCatch(expr, error = \(e) msg <<- paste("error:", conditionMessage(e))),
    warning = \(w) {
      if (msg == "no condition") {
        msg <<- paste("warning:", conditionMessage(w))
      }
      invokeRestart("muffleWarning")
    }
  )
  cat(strwrap(msg, width = 76, exdent = 2), sep = "\n")
}
x <- data.table(a = 1:3, b = c("x", "y", "z"))

# Joins: wrong column, wrong type, accidental many-to-many.
what(x[x, on = "zzz"])
#> error: argument specifying columns received non-existing column(s):
#>   cols[1]='zzz'
what(x[.("x"), on = "a"])
#> error: Incompatible join types: x.a (integer) and i.V1 (character)
what(merge(x, x, by = "zzz"))
#> error: The following columns listed in `by` are missing from x: [zzz]
dup <- data.table(k = c(1, 1, 1), v = 1:3)
what(dup[dup, on = "k"])
#> error: Join results in 9 rows; more than 6 = nrow(x)+nrow(i). Check for
#>   duplicate key values in i each of which join to the same group in x over
#>   and over again. If that's ok, try by=.EACHI to run j for each group to
#>   avoid the large allocation. If you are sure you wish to proceed, rerun
#>   with allow.cartesian=TRUE. Otherwise, please search for this error
#>   message in the FAQ, Wiki, Stack Overflow and data.table issue tracker for
#>   advice.
dup[dup, on = "k", allow.cartesian = TRUE][, .N]
#> [1] 9

# Reshaping.
what(melt(x, id.vars = "zzz"))
#> error: One or more values in 'id.vars' is invalid.
what(dcast(data.table(g = c(1, 1), k = c("u", "u"), v = 1:2), g ~ k,
           value.var = "v"))
#> warning: 'fun.aggregate' is NULL, but found duplicate row/column
#>   combinations, so defaulting to length(). That is, the variables [g, k]
#>   used in 'formula' do not uniquely identify rows in the input 'data'. In
#>   such cases, 'fun.aggregate' is used to derive a single representative
#>   value for each combination in the output data.table, for example by
#>   summing or averaging (fun.aggregate=sum or fun.aggregate=mean,
#>   respectively). Check the resulting table for values larger than 1 to see
#>   which combinations were not unique. See ?dcast.data.table for more
#>   details.

# fifelse() is strict about lengths.
what(fifelse(c(TRUE, FALSE), 1:3, 0L))
#> error: Length of 'yes' is 3 but must be 1 or length of 'test' (2).

# Reading text: a ragged file and a header that is too short.
what(fread(text = "a,b\n1,2\n3,4,5\n6,7"))
#> warning: Stopped early on line 3. Expected 2 fields but found 3. Consider
#>   fill=TRUE. First discarded non-empty line: <<3,4,5>>
what(fread(text = "a,b\n1,2,3\n4,5,6"))
#> warning: Detected 2 column names but the data has 3 columns (i.e. invalid
#>   file). Added an extra default column name for the first column which is
#>   guessed to be row names or an index. Use setnames() afterwards if this
#>   guess is not correct, or fix the file write command that created the file
#>   to create a valid file.

# A data.table made by R itself, not by data.table.
df <- data.frame(x = 1:2)
class(df) <- c("data.table", "data.frame")
what(df[, y := 2L])
#> warning: A shallow copy of this data.table was taken so that := can add or
#>   remove 1 columns by reference. At an earlier point, this data.table was
#>   copied by R (or was created manually using structure() or similar). Avoid
#>   names<- and attr<- which in R currently (and oddly) may copy the whole
#>   data.table. Use set* syntax instead to avoid copying: ?set, ?setnames and
#>   ?setattr. It's also not unusual for data.table-agnostic packages to
#>   produce tables affected by this issue. If this message doesn't help,
#>   please report your use case to the data.table issue tracker so the root
#>   cause can be fixed or this message improved.

Source: data.table package documentation: Joins in data.table

Source: data.table package documentation: Frequently asked questions

A missing file is reported by fread() as an error that starts File 'no-such-file.csv' does not exist or is non-readable and ends with getwd()== and the working directory, which depends on the machine and so is not run here.

Pitfalls

  • DT[, 2] is a data.table, not a vector. A data frame drops a single column to a vector; data.table never does. Use DT[[2]], DT[, col] or DT$col for the vector.

  • b <- a is not a copy. A := or set* call on b changes a too, and so does the same call inside a function that was given a. Use copy() when the original must stay as it is. This is the opposite of the copy-on-modify rule that the rest of R follows (Memory and Copy Semantics).

  • A column wins over a variable. In i, j and by a name is looked up among the columns first, so after year <- 1900 the query DT[year > 2022] still compares the column. Use ..var, env = or a differently named variable.

  • x[y] is a join, and the order matters. x[i, on = ] starts from the rows of i. books[loans, on = "isbn"] has 60 rows, one for each loan, and loans[books, on = "isbn"] starts from the books: a row for each loan of each book, and one row for a book that was never loaned.

  • Check how a join matched. Keys that are not unique give a many-to-many join (an error unless allow.cartesian = TRUE), types that differ give an error, and values that look alike but are not equal (trailing blanks, an ISBN with one digit missing) give NA.

  • rbindlist() binds by position unless told otherwise. use.names = "check" (the default) reports a different order with a message and binds by position. Pass use.names = TRUE.

  • fread() guesses. A column of 13-digit codes is integer64; an empty quoted string stays ""; unquoted blanks are stripped; a date column with one impossible date is a different class from one without. Fix the types with colClasses and check them with vapply(DT, \(x) class(x)[[1L]], character(1)).

  • Sorting is in C-locale. setkey(), setorder() and order() in i sort capitals before lower case in every locale. Sort by the locale of the session with DT[base::order(...)] when that is what is wanted.

  • A function that ends with := may print nothing. Add a trailing [] (see Printing after the := operator).

  • Base replacement functions copy. attr<-, class<- on a data frame and structure() produce tables that := has to repair with a warning (the self-reference warning). Use setattr(), setDT() and setnames().

  • Loops need set(). A for loop of DT[...] calls pays the cost of the bracket on every iteration; set() does not.

  • Packages that use data.table. In a package, import the symbols (import(data.table) or importFrom(data.table, :=, .N)), and declare the columns used in DT[...] to avoid the R CMD check NOTE about "no visible binding for global variable" (assign them NULL or use character names), as the importing vignette describes; see Packages, Libraries and Namespaces and Creating Packages.

Version notes

The table lists the changes that matter for the code on this page, from the NEWS file of the installed data.table 1.18.6.1 (also at https://rdatatable.gitlab.io/data.table/news/index.html). The first rows are the R versions that matter to the page.

Release Change

R 4.0.0

stringsAsFactors = FALSE becomes the default of data.frame(); the default of data.table() is FALSE.

R 4.4.0

base R gets sort_by(), which data.table 1.18.0 extends with a method for data.tables.

R 4.6.0

base R gets %notin%; data.table has had its own since 1.15.0, and attaching the package prints a masking message.

data.table 1.15.0 (Jan 2024)

the env argument and substitute2() for programming; %notin%; nafill() fills the ends for "locf" and "nocb"; setcolorder(before =, after =); shift(type = "cyclic"); melt() with several output columns and NA in measure.vars; fwrite(encoding =) and datatable.fwrite.sep; keyby = TRUE; DT[i, nomatch = NULL] with row numbers; shift() and nafill() error for matrices.

data.table 1.16.0 (Aug 2024)

names(.SD) := lapply(.SD, f); fread(dec = "auto"); fcase(default =) takes a vector and is lazy; showProgress for by; rbindlist() and rbind() bind columns of different but compatible classes, with ignore.attr; setdroplevels() replaces droplevels(in.place = TRUE); measure() and patterns() are exported; R 3.3.0 is the minimum.

data.table 1.17.0 (Feb 2025)

rowwiseDT() builds a small table row by row; fread(logicalYN =); fwrite(compressLevel =); print(DT[, y := 2]) prints; fread() reads Date columns faster, as IDate.

data.table 1.18.0 (Dec 2025)

dcast() is an error when fun.aggregate returns more than one value; melt() returns an integer variable for a list of length one in measure.vars; the hasNA argument of frollmean() and frollsum() becomes has.nf; sort_by() for data.tables; fctr(); cbindlist() and mergelist(); the .selfref.ok() helper; column classes at the bottom of long tables; fread(autostart =), fwrite(logicalAsInt =) and droplevels(in.place =) are removed; R 3.4.0 is the minimum.

data.table 1.18.2.1 (Jan 2026)

set() allocates new column slots itself when it needs them, as := already did.

data.table 1.18.6.1 (Aug 2026)

rows can be deleted by reference with DT[i, .ROW := NULL], and the experimental helper setallocrow() prepares columns for it.

Source: data.table package documentation: NEWS

The 1.18 additions that this page ran are in the next script. The row deletion works only with i (not by), clears the keys and the indices of the table, and is the newest item in the table; the mergelist() call joins a list of tables from left to right with how set to "inner" or "left" (the other modes are "right", "full", "semi", "anti" and "cross").

suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(data.table))
source("scenario.R")
setDT(books)

# data.table 1.18.6.1: rows can be deleted by reference with .ROW := NULL.
# Only i selects the rows (no by), and keys and indices are dropped.
n_before <- nrow(books)
books[is.na(year) | is.na(pages), .ROW := NULL]
c(before = n_before, after = nrow(books))
#> before  after
#>     16     13
books[, .(title, year, pages)][1:3]
#>                   title  year pages
#>                  <char> <int> <int>
#> 1:     The Dispossessed  1974   387
#> 2:  Pride and Prejudice  1813   432
#> 3:   the quiet streets   2019   214

# data.table 1.18.0: a sort_by() method for data.tables (see base R 4.4.0).
sort_by(books[, .(title, year)], ~year)[1:3]
#>                  title  year
#>                 <char> <int>
#> 1: Pride and Prejudice  1813
#> 2:    The Dispossessed  1974
#> 3:    The Lamp at Noon  1999

# data.table 1.18.0: mergelist() joins a list of tables, left to right.
parts <- list(
  data.table(id = 1:3, x = c("a", "b", "c")),
  data.table(id = c(1L, 2L, 4L), y = c("d", "e", "f")),
  data.table(id = c(1L, 3L, 4L), z = c("g", "h", "i"))
)
mergelist(parts, on = "id", how = "inner")
#>       id      x      y      z
#>    <int> <char> <char> <char>
#> 1:     1      a      d      g
mergelist(parts, on = "id", how = "left")
#>       id      x      y      z
#>    <int> <char> <char> <char>
#> 1:     1      a      d      g
#> 2:     2      b      e   <NA>
#> 3:     3      c   <NA>      h

Source: data.table package documentation: mergelist

Where older tutorials differ

Much data.table material on the web predates the 1.15 to 1.18 releases. Most of it still runs; the differences below are the ones a reader will meet.

Older tutorial Current practice Why Version

data.table(..., stringsAsFactors = FALSE) on every call

leave the argument out

its default is FALSE, and since R 4.0.0 so is that of data.frame()

R 4.0.0

a join needs setkey(x, k) first, and x[y] joins the keys

x[y, on = "k"], with keys optional

the help page recommends on = even for keyed tables; on = also allows non-equi and rolling joins

inequalities in on = since 1.9.8

dcast.data.table() and melt.data.table() called by their full names

dcast() and melt()

melt() became a standard generic in 1.15.0 so that other packages can add methods; dcast() is data.table’s own function and accepts a data.table (the full names still work)

1.15.0

append [] to every := to see the result

print(DT[, y := 2]) prints; [] is needed only at the end of a function that ends with :=

the detection of auto-printing was improved in 1.17.0 for the explicit print() case

1.17.0

some older posts attribute the "Invalid .internal.selfref detected" warning to readRDS() or load()

:= and set() work silently on a table read back; the warning marks a table that R copied or that was built by hand

the message of 1.18.6.1 starts "A shallow copy of this data.table was taken"

1.18.6.1

rbind.fill() from plyr, or rbind() that fails on different columns

rbindlist(l, fill = TRUE) or rbind(a, b, fill = TRUE)

both pad the missing columns with NA; use.names = TRUE matches by name

current

eval(parse(text = ...)), get() or bquote() to program on columns

env = list(...) and ..var

env substitutes names safely before evaluation

1.15.0

reshape2::melt() and reshape2::dcast() on a data.table

data.table::melt() and data.table::dcast()

data.table has its own, which take several value columns (measure(), several value.var); the message of data.table’s dcast() calls reshape2 superseded

current

fread(autostart = ), fwrite(logicalAsInt = ) and droplevels(in.place = TRUE)

skip =, fwrite() without the argument, and setdroplevels()

the arguments were removed in 1.18.0 (in.place was deprecated in 1.16.0)

1.18.0

options(datatable.nomatch = )

nomatch = in the query

setting the option has been an error since 1.18.0, after warning from 1.15.0

1.18.0
